name: Chapter 3: Motion in a Plane
description: Vectors, resolution, addition, motion in a plane, projectile motion, relative velocity, uniform circular motion

cards.term: Scalar vs vector?
cards.definition: Scalar: magnitude only (mass, time, temperature). Vector: magnitude and direction, and it obeys the triangle/parallelogram law of addition

cards.term: Is having magnitude and direction enough to be a vector?
cards.definition: No: it must also add by the triangle law. Electric current has a direction but adds like a scalar, so it is a scalar

cards.term: Scalar or vector (NCERT exercises)
cards.definition: Volume, mass, speed, density, moles: scalar; Angular frequency: scalar; Displacement, velocity, acceleration: vector; Angular velocity, impulse: vector; Work, current, pressure, energy: scalar

cards.term: How is a vector written by hand and in print?
cards.definition: An arrow over the letter, \( \vec v \), or bold v. Its magnitude is |v| or v

cards.term: Position vector vs displacement vector?
cards.definition: Position vector r: from the origin to the object. Displacement PP′: from the initial to the final position

cards.term: Does displacement depend on the path taken?
cards.definition: No: only on the end points; every path from P to Q gives the same PQ

cards.term: When are two vectors equal?
cards.definition: Same magnitude and same direction. Shift one parallel to itself: the tails and tips coincide

cards.term: Free vector vs localised vector?
cards.definition: Free: can be shifted parallel to itself without change. Localised: its line of action matters (e.g. a force producing torque)

cards.term: Exercise 3.8: three skaters go from P to Q across a circular rink of radius 200 m by different paths. Displacement of each?
cards.definition: 400 m each; only B (straight along the diameter) has path length = displacement

cards.term: λA for λ > 0 and λ < 0?
cards.definition: λ > 0: same direction, magnitude λ|A|. λ < 0: opposite direction, magnitude |λ||A|

cards.term: Dimensions of λA when λ has units?
cards.definition: Product of the two, e.g. velocity × time = displacement

cards.term: Triangle (head-to-tail) law?
cards.definition: Place the tail of B at the head of A; the resultant R = A + B runs from the tail of A to the head of B

cards.text: Vector addition is {{c1::commutative}} (A + B = B + A) and {{c2::associative}} ((A + B) + C = A + (B + C)).

cards.term: Parallelogram law?
cards.definition: Put A and B tail to tail; the diagonal from the common tail is A + B. Equivalent to the triangle law

cards.term: What is a null (zero) vector? Its properties?
cards.definition: Magnitude 0, direction undefined. A + 0 = A, λ0 = 0, 0A = 0. E.g. displacement after returning to the start

cards.term: How is A − B defined?
cards.definition: \( \vec A - \vec B = \vec A + (-\vec B) \): add the reverse of B

cards.term: Correction: NCERT 3.4 says "as mentioned in section 4.2". Which section?
cards.definition: Section 3.2 (Scalars and vectors). The reference is left over from the old chapter numbering

cards.term: Example 3.1: rain falls at 35 m/s, wind blows east to west at 12 m/s. How should the umbrella be held?
cards.definition: Resultant 37 m/s at tan⁻¹(12/35) ≈ 19° to the vertical; tilt the umbrella towards the east

cards.term: Resolving A along two non-collinear vectors a and b in its plane?
cards.definition: \( \vec A = \lambda \vec a + \mu \vec b \) for suitable real numbers λ, μ

cards.term: What is a unit vector?
cards.definition: A vector of magnitude 1 that only gives a direction; no unit or dimension. \( \hat n = \dfrac{\vec A}{|\vec A|} \)

cards.term: î, ĵ, k̂?
cards.definition: Unit vectors along x, y and z; mutually perpendicular; |î| = |ĵ| = |k̂| = 1

cards.term: Components of A making angle θ with the x-axis?
cards.definition: \( A_x = A\cos\theta,\ A_y = A\sin\theta \)

cards.term: Magnitude and direction from components?
cards.definition: \( A = \sqrt{A_x^2 + A_y^2},\ \tan\theta = \dfrac{A_y}{A_x} \)

cards.term: Is Aₓ a vector?
cards.definition: No: Aₓ is a real number (can be +, − or 0); Aₓî is the vector component

cards.term: 3D components with direction angles α, β, γ?
cards.definition: \( A_x = A\cos\alpha,\ A_y = A\cos\beta,\ A_z = A\cos\gamma,\ A = \sqrt{A_x^2 + A_y^2 + A_z^2} \)

cards.term: Teacher addition: sum of squares of direction cosines?
cards.definition: \( \cos^2\alpha + \cos^2\beta + \cos^2\gamma = 1 \)

cards.term: Exercise 3.19: magnitude and direction of î + ĵ and î − ĵ?
cards.definition: √2 at 45° and √2 at −45° to the x-axis

cards.term: Adding vectors by components?
cards.definition: Add like components: \( R_x = A_x + B_x,\ R_y = A_y + B_y,\ R_z = A_z + B_z \)

cards.term: Why prefer the analytical method?
cards.definition: The graphical method is tedious and less accurate

cards.term: Resultant of A and B at angle θ (law of cosines)?
cards.definition: \( R = \sqrt{A^2 + B^2 + 2AB\cos\theta} \)

cards.term: Direction of the resultant (angle α with A)?
cards.definition: \( \tan\alpha = \dfrac{B\sin\theta}{A + B\cos\theta} \)

cards.term: Law of sines for the vector triangle (Fig. 3.10)?
cards.definition: \( \dfrac{R}{\sin\theta} = \dfrac{A}{\sin\beta} = \dfrac{B}{\sin\alpha} \)

cards.term: Resultant in special cases
cards.definition: θ = 0° (parallel): A + B (maximum); θ = 180° (antiparallel): |A − B| (minimum); θ = 90°: √(A² + B²); A = B, θ = 120°: A (same size as each); A = B, any θ: 2A cos(θ/2)

cards.term: Range of possible resultants of A and B?
cards.definition: \( |A - B| \le R \le A + B \) (Exercise 3.6; equality only for collinear vectors)

cards.term: Example 3.3: boat heads north at 25 km/h; current 10 km/h at 60° east of south. Resultant?
cards.definition: \( R = \sqrt{25^2 + 10^2 + 2(25)(10)\cos 120^\circ} \approx \) 22 km/h, about 23.4° east of north

cards.term: Exercise 3.5(e): can three vectors not in one plane add to zero?
cards.definition: No: the sum of two lies in their plane, so the third must lie there too

cards.term: Exercise 3.7: a + b + c + d = 0. Must each be zero?
cards.definition: No. But |a + c| = |b + d| and |a| ≤ |b| + |c| + |d| are true

cards.term: Position and displacement in a plane?
cards.definition: \( \vec r = x\hat i + y\hat j \), \( \Delta\vec r = \Delta x\,\hat i + \Delta y\,\hat j \)

cards.term: Average velocity in a plane: direction?
cards.definition: Along the displacement Δr (chord), since v̄ = Δr/Δt

cards.term: Direction of instantaneous velocity?
cards.definition: Along the tangent to the path, in the direction of motion

cards.term: Velocity components and magnitude?
cards.definition: \( v_x = \dfrac{dx}{dt},\ v_y = \dfrac{dy}{dt},\ v = \sqrt{v_x^2 + v_y^2},\ \tan\theta = \dfrac{v_y}{v_x} \)

cards.term: Angle between v and a in 1D vs 2D?
cards.definition: 1D: 0° or 180°. In 2D/3D: any angle from 0° to 180°

cards.term: Example 3.4: r = 3.0t î + 2.0t² ĵ + 5.0 k̂. v, a, and v at t = 1 s?
cards.definition: v = 3.0î + 4.0t ĵ; a = 4.0 ĵ m s⁻²; at 1 s: 5.0 m/s at 53° to x

cards.term: Exercise 3.17: r = 3.0t î − 2.0t² ĵ + 4.0 k̂. Speed at t = 2 s?
cards.definition: v = 3î − 8ĵ → 8.54 m/s, 70° below the x-axis; a = −4.0 ĵ

cards.term: Which relations hold for arbitrary motion
cards.definition: v_avg = ½[v(t₁) + v(t₂)]: No (constant a only); v_avg = [r(t₂) − r(t₁)]/(t₂ − t₁): Yes; v(t) = v(0) + at: No; r(t) = r(0) + v(0)t + ½at²: No; a_avg = [v(t₂) − v(t₁)]/(t₂ − t₁): Yes

advancedHtml.frontHtml:

v_avg = [r(t₂) − r(t₁)]/(t₂ − t₁)?
v(t) = v(0) + at?
r(t) = r(0) + v(0)t + ½at²?

True for any motion?

v_avg = ½[v(t₁) + v(t₂)]No (constant a only)
v_avg = [r(t₂) − r(t₁)]/(t₂ − t₁)Yes
v(t) = v(0) + atNo
r(t) = r(0) + v(0)t + ½at²No
a_avg = [v(t₂) − v(t₁)]/(t₂ − t₁)Yes

Definitions always hold; the kinematic equations need constant acceleration.

cards.term: Vector equations for constant acceleration in a plane?
cards.definition: \( \vec v = \vec v_0 + \vec a t,\quad \vec r = \vec r_0 + \vec v_0 t + \tfrac12 \vec a t^2 \)

cards.term: Key idea of 3.8?
cards.definition: Motion in a plane = two independent 1D motions along perpendicular axes, linked only by time

cards.term: Example 3.5: constant acceleration in a plane
cards.definition: t = 6 s from x = 84 m; y = 36 m; speed ≈ 26 m/s

advancedHtml.frontHtml:
Example 3.5

Find the missing step.

Starts at origin with 5.0î m/s; a = (3.0î + 2.0ĵ) m/s². y and speed when x = 84 m?
  1. x = 5t + 1.5t², y = 1.0t²
  2. ?
  3. y = 36 m
  4. v = (5 + 3t)î + 2tĵ = 23î + 12ĵ → 26 m/s
advancedHtml.backHtml:
Example 3.5

Find the missing step.

Starts at origin with 5.0î m/s; a = (3.0î + 2.0ĵ) m/s². y and speed when x = 84 m?
  1. x = 5t + 1.5t², y = 1.0t²
  2. 5t + 1.5t² = 84 → t = 6 s
  3. y = 36 m
  4. v = (5 + 3t)î + 2tĵ = 23î + 12ĵ → 26 m/s

cards.term: Exercise 3.18: from origin with 10ĵ m/s, a = (8î + 2ĵ) m/s². When is x = 16 m? y then?
cards.definition: t = 2 s, y = 24 m, speed 21.26 m/s

cards.term: What is a projectile?
cards.definition: An object in flight after being thrown or projected, moving under gravity alone (air resistance neglected)

cards.term: Who first stated that horizontal and vertical motions of a projectile are independent?
cards.definition: Galileo (Dialogue on the Great World Systems, 1632)

cards.term: Projectile = uniform horizontal motion + vertical free fall
cards.definition: x-shadow moves uniformly (ax = 0); y-shadow rises and falls like a vertical throw (ay = −g); they share only time

advancedHtml.frontHtml:
Projectile · independence of motions

Watch the shadows of a projectile on the two axes. What kind of motion does each shadow do?

Imagine a light above and a light to the side.
advancedHtml.backHtml:
Projectile · independence of motions

Watch the shadows of a projectile on the two axes. What kind of motion does each shadow do?

Horizontal: uniform velocity (aₓ = 0, vₓ = u cos θ).

Vertical: free fall (aᵧ = −g), exactly like a ball thrown straight up with u sin θ.

Both shadows share only the time.

cards.term: Acceleration and initial velocity components of a projectile?
cards.definition: \( a_x = 0,\ a_y = -g;\ \ u_x = u\cos\theta,\ u_y = u\sin\theta \)

cards.term: Position and velocity of a projectile at time t?
cards.definition: \( x = (u\cos\theta)t,\ y = (u\sin\theta)t - \tfrac12 gt^2;\ v_x = u\cos\theta,\ v_y = u\sin\theta - gt \)

cards.term: Equation of trajectory?
cards.definition: \( y = x\tan\theta - \dfrac{g x^2}{2u^2\cos^2\theta} \): form y = ax − bx², a parabola

cards.term: Projectile formulas (ground to ground)
cards.definition: Time to reach the top tₘ: u sin θ / g; Time of flight T: 2u sin θ / g; Maximum height H: u² sin²θ / 2g; Horizontal range R: u² sin 2θ / g; Maximum range: u²/g at θ = 45°

cards.term: Why is T = 2tₘ?
cards.definition: The parabola is symmetric: rising and falling take equal time (same level, no air)

cards.term: Velocity at the highest point?
cards.definition: \( u\cos\theta \), horizontal (vᵧ = 0). Acceleration there is still g downward

cards.term: Speed and angle at landing (same level)?
cards.definition: Speed u again, at θ below the horizontal

cards.term: Minimum speed of a projectile and where?
cards.definition: \( u\cos\theta \) at the top. Minimum kinetic energy = K cos²θ

cards.term: Equal ranges for complementary angles; maximum at 45°
cards.definition: R = u² sin 2θ / g: θ and 90° − θ give the same range; 45° gives the maximum u²/g

advancedHtml.frontHtml:
Projectile · complementary angles

Same launch speed at 15°, 30°, 45°, 60°, 75°. Which angles land at the same spot, and which goes farthest?

Think it through, then flip.

cards.term: Example 3.6: prove that 45° + α and 45° − α give equal ranges.
cards.definition: sin 2θ = sin(90° ± 2α) = cos 2α for both

cards.term: Teacher addition: relation between range and maximum height?
cards.definition: \( R = 4H\cot\theta \); at θ = 45°, \( H = R/4 \)

cards.term: Teacher addition: projectiles at θ and 90° − θ (same u). Product of their times of flight?
Example 3.8: cricket ball at 28 m/s, 30° above horizontal. H, T, R?
cards.definition: H = 10.0 m, T = 2.9 s, R = 69 m

cards.term: Exercise 3.13: a cricketer can throw 100 m at most. How high can he throw the same ball?
cards.definition: 50 m (u²/g = 100 m; H = u²/2g)

cards.term: Ball under a 25 m ceiling
cards.definition: Choose θ so that H = 25 m (θ ≈ 33.6°), then R ≈ 150.5 m

advancedHtml.frontHtml:
Exercise 3.12

Find the missing step.

Ceiling 25 m high, ball thrown at 40 m/s. Max horizontal distance without hitting the ceiling?
  1. Set H = 25: u² sin²θ / 2g = 25
  2. ?
  3. R = u² sin 2θ / g = 1600 × sin 67.2° / 9.8
  4. R ≈ 150.5 m
advancedHtml.backHtml:
Exercise 3.12

Find the missing step.

Ceiling 25 m high, ball thrown at 40 m/s. Max horizontal distance without hitting the ceiling?
  1. Set H = 25: u² sin²θ / 2g = 25
  2. sin²θ = 2 × 9.8 × 25 / 1600 = 0.306 → θ ≈ 33.6°
  3. R = u² sin 2θ / g = 1600 × sin 67.2° / 9.8
  4. R ≈ 150.5 m

cards.term: Thrown horizontally at u from height h: time to reach the ground?
cards.definition: \( t = \sqrt{\dfrac{2h}{g}} \), independent of u

cards.term: Thrown horizontally at u from height h: horizontal distance?
cards.definition: \( x = u\sqrt{\dfrac{2h}{g}} \)

cards.term: Example 3.7: stone thrown horizontally at 15 m/s from a 490 m cliff. Time and impact speed?
cards.definition: 10 s; vᵧ = 98 m/s, speed = √(15² + 98²) ≈ 99 m/s

cards.term: One ball is dropped and another thrown horizontally from the same height at the same time. Which lands first?
cards.definition: Together: vertical motion is identical (uᵧ = 0 for both)

cards.term: Trap: does a projectile’s path depend only on its acceleration?
cards.definition: No: the same g gives a straight line (thrown vertically) or a parabola, depending on the initial velocity

cards.term: Resultant velocity vs relative velocity?
cards.definition: Resultant: an object with two velocities has v = v₁ + v₂. Relative: v₁₂ = v₁ − v₂ (velocity of 1 as seen from 2)

cards.term: Rain falls vertically; you walk forward. Which way should you tilt the umbrella?
cards.definition: Forward: the rain relative to you is v_rain − v_you, which slants towards you

cards.term: Crossing a river of width d in the least time: heading and time?
cards.definition: Head perpendicular to the bank; t = d/vʙ; drift = vᵣd/vʙ

cards.term: Crossing a river along the shortest path (straight across): heading?
cards.definition: Upstream at angle θ to the normal with \( \sin\theta = \dfrac{v_r}{v_b} \); time \( \dfrac{d}{\sqrt{v_b^2 - v_r^2}} \)

cards.term: Trap: can a boat reach the opposite point if the river is faster than the boat?
cards.definition: No: sin θ = vᵣ/vʙ > 1 is impossible; it will always drift downstream

cards.term: What is uniform circular motion?
cards.definition: Motion in a circle at constant speed

cards.term: Uniform circular motion: directions of v and a
cards.definition: v tangent, a = v²/R towards the centre (perpendicular to v); acceleration exists because the direction of v changes

advancedHtml.frontHtml:
Uniform circular motion · intuition

A ball goes round a circle at constant speed. Which way do its velocity and acceleration point, and is it accelerating at all?

Constant speed… so is a = 0?
advancedHtml.backHtml:
Uniform circular motion · intuition

A ball goes round a circle at constant speed. Which way do its velocity and acceleration point, and is it accelerating at all?

v is along the tangent; a = v²/R points to the centre, always ⟂ v.

Speed is constant but the direction of v keeps turning, so the ball is accelerating. a has constant size but is not a constant vector.

cards.term: Magnitude and direction of centripetal acceleration?
cards.definition: \( a_c = \dfrac{v^2}{R} = \omega^2 R \), towards the centre

cards.term: How is v²/R derived (Fig. 3.18)?
cards.definition: Triangles of position vectors and velocity vectors are similar: |Δv|/v = |Δr|/R, and |Δr| ≈ vΔt

cards.term: Is centripetal acceleration a constant vector?
cards.definition: No: constant magnitude, but its direction keeps changing

cards.term: Can the kinematic equations be used for uniform circular motion?
cards.definition: No: acceleration is not constant in direction

cards.term: Who named centripetal acceleration, and who first published its analysis?
cards.definition: Newton named it ("centre-seeking"); Huygens published the analysis in 1673

cards.term: Define angular speed and relate it to v.
cards.definition: \( \omega = \dfrac{\Delta\theta}{\Delta t} \) ; \( v = R\omega \)

cards.term: ω, v, a in terms of frequency ν?
cards.definition:
\( \omega = 2\pi
u,\ v = 2\pi R
u,\ a_c = 4\pi^2
u^2 R \)

cards.term: Example 3.9: insect in a 12 cm groove makes 7 revolutions in 100 s. ω, v, a?
cards.definition: ω = 0.44 rad/s, v = 5.3 cm/s, a = 2.3 cm/s² (not a constant vector)

cards.term: Exercise 3.14: stone on an 80 cm string makes 14 revolutions in 25 s. Acceleration?
cards.definition: 9.9 m s⁻² along the radius, towards the centre

cards.term: Exercise 3.15: aircraft loop of radius 1.00 km at 900 km/h. a_c compared with g?
cards.definition: a = 250²/1000 = 62.5 m s⁻² ≈ 6.4 g

cards.term: Is the net acceleration in any circular motion towards the centre?
cards.definition: Only if the speed is constant. If speed changes, there is also a tangential component

cards.term: Exercise 3.16(c): average acceleration over one full cycle of uniform circular motion?
cards.definition: Zero (the velocity returns to its starting value)

cards.term: Exercise 3.9: cyclist goes O → P (1 km), a quarter circle, then back to O in 10 min. Displacement, average velocity, average speed?
cards.definition: 0, 0, and (2 + π/2) km ÷ 1/6 h ≈ 21.4 km/h

cards.term: Exercise 3.11: cab takes 23 km in 28 min to reach a hotel 10 km away. Average speed and |average velocity|?
cards.definition: 49.3 km/h and 21.4 km/h; equal only for a straight path

cards.term: Exercise 3.22: aircraft at 3400 m; positions 10 s apart subtend 30° at an observer. Speed?
cards.definition: Distance = 2 × 3400 tan 15° ≈ 1822 m → 182 m/s

cards.term: What makes a quantity a scalar
cards.definition: is conserved in a process: False (e.g. KE in inelastic collision); can never be negative: False (temperature in °C); must be dimensionless: False (mass); does not vary in space: False (temperature); is the same for observers with rotated axes: True
